claim: Neural populations from various sensory regions demonstrate dynamic range adaptation in response to changes in the statistical distribution of their input stimuli.
source: Neural populations from various sensory regions demonstrate dynamic range adaptation in response to changes in the statistical distribution of their input stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory systems supported by the broader literature context and citations provided later in the manuscript.

claim: Dynamic range adaptations in sensory regions help optimize the transmission of information about sensory inputs.
source: These adaptations help optimize the transmission of information about sensory inputs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established understanding in the field.

claim: Neurons in primary motor cortex exhibited a change in the amplitude of their directional tuning curves between two- and three-dimensional tasks.
source: We found that neurons in primary motor cortex exhibited a change in the amplitude of their directional tuning curves between the two tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tuning changes in primary motor cortex are most consistent with dynamic range adaptation.
source: We then leveraged the simultaneous nature of the recordings to test several hypotheses about the population-based mechanisms driving these changes and found that the results are most consistent with dynamic range adaptation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data analysis comparing multiple hypotheses.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation is not limited to sensory regions.
source: Our results demonstrate that dynamic range adaptation is neither limited to sensory regions nor to rescaling of monotonic stimulus intensity tuning curves, but may rather represent a canonical feature of neural encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in motor cortex.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation is not limited to rescaling of monotonic stimulus intensity tuning curves.
source: Our results demonstrate that dynamic range adaptation is neither limited to sensory regions nor to rescaling of monotonic stimulus intensity tuning curves, but may rather represent a canonical feature of neural encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing adaptation in directional tuning.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation may represent a canonical feature of neural encoding.
source: Our results demonstrate that dynamic range adaptation is neither limited to sensory regions nor to rescaling of monotonic stimulus intensity tuning curves, but may rather represent a canonical feature of neural encoding.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Neurons in primary visual cortex and the retina encode the intensity of light with their firing rates.
source: Neurons in primary visual cortex and the retina encode the intensity of light with their firing rates (Kuffler, 1953; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Neural tuning curves in visual cortex shift and adjust their slopes when light intensity changes to provide resolution over the new range of light intensity.
source: When the level of light intensity changes from the dark theater to the bright lobby, the neural tuning curves shift and adjust their slopes to provide resolution over the new range of light intensity (Shapley and Enroth-Cugell, 1984; Ohzawa et al., 1985; Smirnakis et al., 1997; Ohzawa et al., 1982; Harris et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation has been documented in auditory systems.
source: In addition to this example in the visual system, dynamic range adaptation has also been documented in other sensory areas, including the auditory (Kvale and Schreiner, 2004; Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Dean et al., 2005; Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Rabinowitz et al., 2011) and somatosensory (Maravall et al., 2007; Katz et al., 2006) systems.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation has been documented in somatosensory systems.
source: In addition to this example in the visual system, dynamic range adaptation has also been documented in other sensory areas, including the auditory (Kvale and Schreiner, 2004; Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Dean et al., 2005; Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Rabinowitz et al., 2011) and somatosensory (Maravall et al., 2007; Katz et al., 2006) systems.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation optimizes the transmission of information about input stimuli within the limited tuning ranges of neurons.
source: This phenomenon has been described as optimizing the transmission of information about input stimuli within the limited tuning ranges of the neurons (Brenner et al., 2000; Fairhall et al., 2001; Wark et al., 2007; Atick, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Firing rates of neurons in primary motor cortex modulate with output force levels in monotonic relationships.
source: Force was one of the earliest output variables described, and many studies have demonstrated that firing rates of neurons in primary motor cortex (M1) modulate with output force levels in monotonic relationships (Evarts, 1966, 1968; Humphrey et al., 1970; Hepp-Reymond et al., 1978; Georgopoulos et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Humphrey et al. noted that regression coefficients relating motor neuronal activity to force scaled with the range of forces in their task.
source: Humphrey et al. briefly noted in their work that the value of regression coefficients relating motor neuronal activity to force scaled with the range of forces in their task (Humphrey et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Motor cortical neurons encoding force during an isometric pinching task undergo dynamic range adaptation with changes in task context and cued expectation.
source: They demonstrated that motor cortical neurons encoding force during an isometric pinching task undergo dynamic range adaptation with changes in the task context and cued expectation of the task context.
evidence: This refers to work by Hepp-Reymond et al. and is supported by citation.

claim: Motor cortical neurons demonstrate a cosine-tuning relationship between movement direction and neuronal firing rates.
source: These studies demonstrated a cosine-tuning relationship between movement direction and neuronal firing rates.
evidence: This refers to studies by Georgopoulos et al. and others, supported by citations.

claim: Each motor cortical unit has a preferred direction where the firing rate is maximal for movements in that direction and minimal for movements in the opposite direction.
source: Each unit was described as having a preferred direction where the firing rate was maximal for movements in that direction and minimal for movements in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a description of the classical cosine tuning model.

claim: The classical cosine tuning model predicts a lower range in firing rates for 2D movements than 3D movements when the preferred direction is not coplanar with the 2D movement space.
source: Notably, the model predicts a lower range in firing rates for 2D movements than 3D movements when the preferred direction is not coplanar with the 2D movement space.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the cosine tuning model.

claim: The average size of the overlapping population of units contributing to cursor movement in both contexts was 26.4 units for Monkey A and 37.2 units for Monkey C.
source: The average size of this overlapping population was 26.4 units for Monkey A (min: 13; max: 32) and 37.2 units for Monkey C (min: 30; max: 45).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: For five recording sessions from Monkey A and 4 from Monkey C, the entire population of units controlling cursor movement was identical between the two contexts.
source: For five recording sessions from Monkey A and 4 from Monkey C, the entire population of units controlling the cursor movement was identical between the two contexts.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental conditions.

claim: Six units that appeared to lose signal during the recording session were removed from analyses.
source: Six units that appeared to lose signal during the recording session were removed from these analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The range of firing rates for all 16 targets during the 2D context approaches, and occasionally exceeds, the range observed for all 26 targets during the 3D context.
source: Instead, the range of firing rates for all 16 targets during the 2D context approaches, and occasionally exceeds, the range observed for all 26 targets during the 3D context.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Units show greater maximal firing rates and lower minimal firing rates in the 2D context compared to the 3D context for the BCI task.
source: The units show greater maximal firing rates and lower minimal firing rates in the 2D context compared to the 3D context for the BCI task.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The azimuthal preferred directions are nearly the same between the 2D and 3D contexts.
source: As expected, the azimuthal preferred directions are nearly the same between the two contexts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The changes in azimuthal preferred directions are insignificant under the Moore test of paired samples of angles for both monkeys.
source: The changes in azimuthal preferred directions are insignificant under the Moore test of paired samples of angles for both monkeys (Moore, 1980; Zar, 2010).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: 334 of 471 units in Monkey A exhibited an increase in planar tuning range in the 2D context relative to the 3D context.
source: We found that 334 of 471 units in Monkey A and 230 of 409 units in Monkey C exhibited an increase in planar tuning range in the 2D context relative to the 3D context.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: 230 of 409 units in Monkey C exhibited an increase in planar tuning range in the 2D context relative to the 3D context.
source: We found that 334 of 471 units in Monkey A and 230 of 409 units in Monkey C exhibited an increase in planar tuning range in the 2D context relative to the 3D context.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: Similar tuning changes occur when the order of 2D and 3D contexts is reversed.
source: While Figure 2D shows the tuning difference when the 2D context follows the 3D context, we found that similar tuning changes occur when the order is reversed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The tuning range changes are individually significant for both PVA and OLE decoder types.
source: When we separately looked at sessions using either the PVA decoder or the OLE decoder, we found that the results were individually significant for both decoder types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Similar changes in tuning range occur when the entire population used to control cursor movement was identical between the two contexts.
source: When we looked at the population response from these sessions, we again found similar changes in tuning range (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There was a slight decrease in tuning ranges for repeats of the 2D context for Monkey A.
source: We found a slight decrease in the tuning ranges for repeats of the 2D context for Monkey A and repeats of the 3D context for Monkey C: the second presentation tended to have decreased tuning relative to the first.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: There was a slight decrease in tuning ranges for repeats of the 3D context for Monkey C.
source: We found a slight decrease in the tuning ranges for repeats of the 2D context for Monkey A and repeats of the 3D context for Monkey C: the second presentation tended to have decreased tuning relative to the first.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The decrease in tuning on repeated presentations may be due to fatigue or satiation.
source: This may be due to fatigue or satiation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed decrease.

claim: Under the re-aiming mechanism, units would undergo either an increase or decrease in tuning range, depending on the elevation of the unit's preferred direction relative to the elevation of the re-aiming point.
source: With this mechanism, units would undergo either an increase or decrease in tuning range, depending on the elevation of the unit's preferred direction relative to the elevation of the re-aiming point.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the re-aiming hypothesis.

claim: Under the speed gain mechanism, the relative change in tuning range is identical for all units.
source: Unlike the re-aiming mechanism, the relative change in tuning range expected does not vary with preferred direction. Instead, the relative change in tuning range is identical for all units.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the speed gain hypothesis.

claim: The data exhibit a dose-response effect predicted by dynamic range adaptation.
source: We find our data to be most consistent with the dynamic range adaptation mechanism. Two pieces of evidence suggest this. First, our data exhibit the dose-response effect predicted only by dynamic range adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is no evidence of coordinated, opposing changes in dynamic range for neurons whose 3D preferred directions were mirrored across the xy-plane, as predicted by the re-aiming mechanism.
source: Second, we find no evidence of coordinated, opposing changes in dynamic range for neurons whose 3D preferred directions were mirrored across the xy-plane, as predicted by the re-aiming mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis.

claim: When fitting a weighted linear regression to the ratio of 3D planar to 2D ranges against the absolute value of the elevation angle, significant negative slopes were found for both monkeys.
source: When we fit a weighted linear regression to these data, we found significant, negative slopes, indicating that neurons tuned to larger elevation angles show larger dynamic range changes between 2D and 3D (Monkey A: P<10-12, F-test; Monkey C, P=0.00125).
evidence: This is a statistical result from data analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Neurons tuned to larger elevation angles show larger dynamic range changes between 2D and 3D.
source: When we fit a weighted linear regression to these data, we found significant, negative slopes, indicating that neurons tuned to larger elevation angles show larger dynamic range changes between 2D and 3D (Monkey A: P<10-12, F-test; Monkey C, P=0.00125).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: More than half of the units (54.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey A.
source: When we compared the full tuning ranges from the 2D and 3D contexts, we found that more than half of the units (54.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey A, whereas less than half of the units (41.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey C (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Less than half of the units (41.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey C.
source: When we compared the full tuning ranges from the 2D and 3D contexts, we found that more than half of the units (54.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey A, whereas less than half of the units (41.8%) had greater full tuning range in 2D than 3D for Monkey C (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For Monkey A, of the 87 units predicted to increase tuning range under re-aiming, 66 were observed to increase.
source: For Monkey A, of the 87 units predicted to increase tuning range, 66 were observed to increase.
evidence: This is a direct report of results from the re-aiming analysis.

claim: For Monkey A, of the 55 units predicted to decrease tuning range under re-aiming, only eight were observed to do so.
source: Of the 55 units predicted to decrease tuning range, only eight were observed to do so.
evidence: This is a direct report of results from the re-aiming analysis.

claim: For Monkey C, of the 86 units predicted to increase tuning range under re-aiming, 57 were observed to increase.
source: For Monkey C, of the 86 units predicted to increase tuning range, 57 were observed to increase.
evidence: This is a direct report of results from the re-aiming analysis.

claim: For Monkey C, of the 72 units predicted to decrease tuning range under re-aiming, only 30 were observed to do so.
source: Of the 72 units predicted to decrease tuning range, only 30 were observed to do so.
evidence: This is a direct report of results from the re-aiming analysis.

claim: In both monkeys, more than half of the neurons predicted to show decreases in dynamic range under re-aiming actually showed increases in dynamic range.
source: In both monkeys, more than half of the neurons predicted to show decreases in dynamic range from the 3D context to the 2D under the re-aiming mechanism actually showed increases in dynamic range, as predicted by the dynamic range adaptation mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the re-aiming analysis results.

claim: The adaptation process appeared to occur rapidly with the switch from the 3D to 2D context.
source: The adaptation process appeared to occur rapidly with the switch from the 3D to 2D context.
evidence: This is supported by the timecourse analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The exponential decay coefficient for the reduction in 2D model error was 5.3 (3.2, 16.7) trials for Monkey A.
source: We fit exponential models to the reduction in 2D model error for each monkey, and found exponential decay coefficients (with 95% confidence bounds) of 5.3 (3.2, 16.7) trials for Monkey A and 4.6 (3.2, 10.5) trials for Monkey C.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The exponential decay coefficient for the reduction in 2D model error was 4.6 (3.2, 10.5) trials for Monkey C.
source: We fit exponential models to the reduction in 2D model error for each monkey, and found exponential decay coefficients (with 95% confidence bounds) of 5.3 (3.2, 16.7) trials for Monkey A and 4.6 (3.2, 10.5) trials for Monkey C.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The retuning effect nears completion within seconds.
source: Because each trial takes approximately 1 s to perform, the retuning effect nears completion within seconds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the exponential decay coefficients and trial duration.

claim: The means of the adaptation completeness metrics are 0.5157 (±0.1121) for Monkey A and 0.6793 (±0.1233) for Monkey C.
source: Furthermore, the means (±SE) of the metrics are 0.5157 (±0.1121) for Monkey A and 0.6793 (±0.1233) for Monkey C.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dynamic range adaptation is more than halfway complete for both monkeys.
source: These results suggest that the dynamic range adaptation is more than halfway complete for both monkeys.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the adaptation completeness metrics.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation is not always complete, even in sensory systems.
source: It is worthwhile to note that dynamic range adaptation is not always complete, even in sensory systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to work in auditory and visual systems.

claim: No evidence of dynamic range adaptation was observed in the hand-control version of the task.
source: Unlike with the BCI task, we see no evidence of dynamic range adaptation in the hand-control version of this task.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: BCI provides a powerful framework for addressing basic scientific questions about motor control because the effect each neuron has on cursor movement is fully specified by the experimenter.
source: BCI provides a powerful framework for addressing basic scientific questions about motor control, including the dynamic range adaptation effects observed here, because the effect each neuron has on cursor movement is fully specified by the experimenter, and because we can obviate complicating factors such as gravity and inertia (Golub et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of BCI for research, supported by citation.

claim: BCI allows researchers to obviate complicating factors such as gravity and inertia.
source: BCI provides a powerful framework for addressing basic scientific questions about motor control, including the dynamic range adaptation effects observed here, because the effect each neuron has on cursor movement is fully specified by the experimenter, and because we can obviate complicating factors such as gravity and inertia (Golub et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of BCI for research, supported by citation.

claim: The time scale of dynamic range adaptation is on the order of seconds.
source: First, the time scale of dynamic range adaptation is on the order of seconds (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The time scale of BCI-learning-related changes in neural tuning is on the order of tens of minutes to days.
source: The time scale of BCI-learning-related changes in neural tuning is on the order of tens of minutes (Jarosiewicz et al., 2008; Chase et al., 2012) to days (Ganguly and Carmena, 2009; Ganguly et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation is restricted to changes in tuning depth; changes in preferred direction are minimal.
source: Second, the dynamic range adaptation is restricted to changes in tuning depth; changes in preferred direction are minimal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data analysis.

claim: In BCI learning studies, preferred directions typically change as well.
source: In BCI learning studies, preferred directions typically change as well.
evidence: This is a statement about BCI learning studies, supported by general knowledge and citations.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation occurs without any overt learning pressure.
source: Third, dynamic range adaptation occurs without any overt learning pressure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design.

claim: If the subject continued using the same firing rates in the 3D and 2D contexts, performance would have been unaffected.
source: In studies of BCI learning, the mapping between neural activity and cursor movements is changed in such a way to impair task performance. That was not the case here: if the subject continued using the same firing rates in the 3D and 2D contexts, performance would have been unaffected.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental design.

claim: Dynamic range adaptation represents an additional degree of flexibility in the responses of neurons in the motor system.
source: For these reasons, we speculate that dynamic range adaptation represents an additional degree of flexibility in the responses of neurons in the motor system.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: In hand control, hundreds of thousands of neurons likely contribute to arm movements, and the overall change in dynamic range might be distributed over all of them, making them difficult to observe.
source: In hand control, hundreds of thousands of neurons likely contribute to arm movements, and the overall change in dynamic range might be distributed over all of them, making them difficult to observe.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed adaptation in hand control.

claim: In BCI, only the recorded neurons contribute to cursor movement, which could potentially make the effect easier to see.
source: In BCI, only the recorded neurons contribute to cursor movement, which could potentially make the effect easier to see.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why adaptation is observed in BCI.

claim: The number of movement parameters that an individual neuron tunes for in hand control is quite large, and when moving from 3D to 2D, the percentage change in number of control parameters is small.
source: Another possibility is that the number of movement parameters that an individual neuron tunes for in hand control is quite large, and when moving from 3D to 2D, the percentage change in number of control parameters is small.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed adaptation in hand control.

claim: Hand control and BCI movements may invoke fundamentally different control schemes.
source: A third intriguing possibility is that hand control and BCI movements invoke fundamentally different control schemes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: It is possible that dynamic range adaptation in the motor system only occurs under conditions of changing force.
source: It is possible that dynamic range adaptation in the motor system only occurs under conditions of changing force.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: Isometric force production may be a closer analog to BCI than overt reaching movements.
source: If this is true, it suggests that isometric force production is a closer analog to BCI than the overt reaching movements to which it is typically compared.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparison of results.

claim: Directional tuning is stable across repetitions within the same condition.
source: Although directional tuning has been shown to change in a context-dependent manner, it should be emphasized that directional tuning is stable across repetitions within the same condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the stability of directional tuning.

claim: Tuning function changes of preferred direction and modulation depth have been observed between brain control and hand control.
source: Tuning function changes of preferred direction and modulation depth have been observed between brain control and hand control (Taylor et al., 2002; Carmena et al., 2003; Lebedev et al., 2005), between movements in different speed ranges (Moran and Schwartz, 1999; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007), and between movements in different postures (Scott and Kalaska, 1995; Sergio and Kalaska, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Tuning can change during learning when adapting to visuomotor perturbations.
source: Tuning can change during learning, when adapting to visuomotor perturbations (Wise et al., 1998; Paz et al., 2003; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2009), force field perturbations (Gandolfo et al., 2000; Arce et al., 2010), BCI decoder changes (Jarosiewicz et al., 2008; Ganguly and Carmena, 2009; Hwang et al., 2013), or even the consistent coupling of sensory cues with rewarded actions (Zach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Using a principle of information processing, the tuning curves from the 2D context may be predicted from the 3D context.
source: One feature that distinguishes dynamic range adaptation from these other sorts of tuning changes is that, using a principle of information processing (namely, that the total range of firing is rescaled according to the output statistics), the tuning curves from the 2D context may be predicted from the 3D context.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the predictability of dynamic range adaptation.

claim: Certain types of dynamic range adaptation, such as contrast gain normalization in the visual system, have been linked to a divisive normalization mechanism.
source: Certain types of dynamic range adaptation, such as contrast gain normalization in the visual system, have been linked to a divisive normalization mechanism (Carandini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Neurons in M1 serve to efficiently transmit contextually encoded information.
source: These results support the hypothesis that neurons in M1 serve to efficiently transmit contextually encoded information.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Motor learning in dynamic environments can be viewed as learning efficient ways to encode information.
source: Motor learning in dynamic environments can be viewed as learning efficient ways to encode information.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about motor learning.

claim: Changes in environmental context, such as tool use, can lead to changes in the association between M1 activity and motor output.
source: Changes in the environmental context, such as tool use, can lead to changes in the association between M1 activity and motor output (Quallo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The common linear tuning function maximizes the output entropy for a uniform distribution of target directions in a 3D environment.
source: The common linear tuning function (Georgopoulos et al., 1982) maximizes the output entropy for a uniform distribution of target directions in a 3D environment.
evidence: This is a statement about information theory applied to neural tuning, supported by citation.

claim: Histogram equalization maximizes the information transmission in the low-noise limit.
source: This 'histogram equalization' maximizes the information transmission in the low-noise limit (Nadal and Parga, 1994; Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The population adaptively displays new coding schemes that fully utilize the ranges of the units comprising the population.
source: Rather than using a subset of the available tuning ranges, the population adaptively displays new coding schemes that fully utilize the ranges of the units comprising the population.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Adaptive learning of the M1 population allows for the efficient encoding of task relevant information in changing environments.
source: This adaptive learning of the M1 population allows for the efficient encoding of task relevant information in changing environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Two male Rhesus macaques were trained to perform a center-out reaching task in a 3D virtual environment.
source: Briefly, two male Rhesus monkeys were trained to perform a center-out reaching task in a 3D virtual environment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Both monkeys were implanted with a 96-channel array.
source: Both monkeys were implanted with a 96-channel array (Cyberkinetics Neurotechnology Systems, Inc.).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The implantations were visually placed in the proximal arm area of primary motor cortex.
source: The implantations were visually placed in the proximal arm area of primary motor cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: There were 26 targets in the 3D context and 16 targets in the 2D context.
source: There were 26 targets in the 3D context and 16 targets in the 2D context.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The two target sets included eight common targets, allowing for direct comparison of tuning between the two task contexts.
source: The two target sets included eight common targets, allowing for direct comparison of tuning between the two task contexts (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: 18 sessions from Monkey A and 11 from Monkey C were analyzed.
source: We analyzed 18 sessions from Monkey A and 11 from Monkey C.
evidence: This is a description of the data analyzed.

claim: Cursor movement was updated online every 33 ms with outputs from the decoders.
source: With the fitted models of neural activity, cursor movement was updated online every 33 ms with outputs from the decoders as described in more detail in the Materials and methods section.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: For the 2D task, the z-component of the decoded movement was zeroed to constrain movement to the xy-plane.
source: For the 2D task, the z-component of the decoded movement was zeroed to constrain movement to the xy-plane.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
